lesson.title: Domain Analysis: Drawing the Boundaries Before You Sketch
lesson.summary: Before any curve can be sketched, its domain has to be pinned down exactly, since every forbidden input becomes a vertical asymptote, a hole, or a boundary point later in the analysis.
lesson.body:
Domain analysis is always the first step of curve sketching, and it earns that position because every later step depends on it. An intercept that falls outside the domain is not a real intercept. An asymptote candidate that falls outside the domain does not exist. And an endpoint of a restricted domain is a genuine candidate for an extreme value, exactly the situation covered by endpoint extrema, so getting the domain wrong at the start can quietly corrupt every step that follows.

Three restriction types come up constantly. A denominator cannot equal zero, so any rational expression excludes the x-values that make its denominator vanish. An even-indexed root (square root, fourth root, and so on) requires a nonnegative value underneath it, so the radicand must be greater than or equal to zero. A logarithm requires a strictly positive argument, so whatever is inside the log must be greater than zero, not just nonnegative.

Consider f(x) = sqrt(x + 3)/(x - 1). Two restrictions apply at once here. The square root requires x + 3 ≥ 0, meaning x ≥ -3. The denominator requires x ≠ 1. Combining both conditions gives the domain [-3, 1) ∪ (1, infinity). Notice what each restriction produces downstream. At x = -3, the function is defined, f(-3) = sqrt(0)/(-4) = 0, so this is a closed, included endpoint of the domain; if this function were being analyzed for extreme values on this restricted domain, x = -3 would be a genuine endpoint candidate to check, exactly as in endpoint extrema. At x = 1, the function is undefined, and since the numerator sqrt(4) = 2 is nonzero there, this is a true vertical asymptote rather than a removable hole, a fact that becomes essential once you get to asymptote analysis.

That hole-versus-asymptote distinction deserves its own quick example, because it is the most common domain mistake. Let g(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2). Before simplifying, the domain excludes x = 2, since that makes the denominator zero. Algebraically, the expression simplifies to g(x) = x + 2 for every x except x = 2, since x^2 - 4 factors as (x - 2)(x + 2) and the (x - 2) cancels. But that cancellation happens only where x ≠ 2 to begin with; the simplified formula x + 2 is perfectly well defined at x = 2 (it gives 4), yet the original function g is not, because the domain restriction was locked in before any simplifying happened. The graph of g is the line y = x + 2 with a single point missing at (2, 4), a hole rather than an asymptote, since the offending factor cancels completely rather than surviving in the denominator.

Logarithms bring a different flavor of restriction. Let h(x) = ln(4 - x^2). The argument must be strictly positive: 4 - x^2 > 0, which rearranges to x^2 < 4, giving the open interval -2 < x < 2. This domain has no included endpoints at all, since the inequality is strict. That has a real consequence for extreme-value analysis: because neither x = -2 nor x = 2 belongs to the domain, neither one can ever be an endpoint extremum, no matter how the function behaves nearby. Domain analysis is what tells you, before you do any other work, whether endpoint behavior is even on the table.
